gly.start.text_dramatic: The glucose molecule slips into the cell's interior, and you ride inside it — one carbon among six, carried into the cytosol where the sugar is spent. A ten-enzyme production line waits here, primed for exactly this molecule. The journey begins: glucose at one end, pyruvate at the other, and ten steps between — every one of them will ask something of you.
gly.start.text_teaching: Glycolysis is the catabolic process in which glucose is converted into pyruvate via ten enzymatic steps. The ten steps run in two phases: a priming phase that requires an input of energy — 2 ATPs per glucose — and a payoff phase in which energy is released in the form of 4 ATPs, 2 per glyceraldehyde molecule. The full ledger for one glucose: a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. That is the engine this whole story rides.

gly.g6p.text_dramatic: The trap closes. Hexokinase takes hold of the glucose and bolts a phosphate onto its sixth carbon — a charged handle the sugar cannot shed. What drifted in as loose fuel is now glucose-6-phosphate: claimed, marked, and held by the cell that caught it. The road back out is gone; the only way leads deeper.
gly.g6p.text_teaching: Step 1: alpha-D-glucose is phosphorylated at the 6 carbon by ATP via the enzyme hexokinase (class: transferase), yielding alpha-D-glucose-6-phosphate — glucose + ATP -> glucose-6-phosphate + ADP. This is a regulatory step, negatively regulated by the presence of glucose-6-phosphate itself: when the cell's G6P pool is full, hexokinase eases off (product inhibition). The phosphate is the cell's grip — once the fuel carries a charge, it stays in the cell's economy.

gly.pfk.text_dramatic: Phosphofructokinase — the gatekeeper. This is the step the cell welded shut behind you: fructose-6-phosphate takes a second phosphate and becomes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and past this gate there is no walking back up. The sugar is committed to the burn. But look closely at the enzyme on screen — for in some hosts the gatekeeper is born broken, and the whole road jams at the step that was meant to be irreversible.
gly.pfk.text_teaching: Step 3: phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate at the 1-carbon position — fructose-6-phosphate + ATP -> fructose-1,6-bisphosphate + ADP. This is the committed step of glycolysis because of its large ΔG value: once this reaction runs, the molecule is locked onto the glycolysis road. The cast on screen is PDB 4PFK — phosphofructokinase from the bacterium Geobacillus stearothermophilus, resolved at 2.40 Å (Evans, Farrants, Hudson 1981) — a bacterial stand-in for the human enzyme, shown honestly as such. The disease story is carried in text: the featured human mutation, PFKM G209D, abolishes PFK-1 activity in yeast-complementation assays (Raben 1995) and is classified Likely pathogenic in ClinVar (VCV003375341) for Glycogen Storage Disease VII / Tarui disease (MIM:232800). Residue 209 is human PFKM numbering; the bacterial 4PFK has no sourced equivalent at that position (its own residue 209 is a histidine), so the game asserts no on-structure mutation here — the enzyme you see is the healthy cast, and the Tarui story is the frame this node carries. The restoration arc that follows is the game's staged replay of a corrected enzyme: a narrative reveal, taught honestly at the next branch node.

choices.label: Try to edit PFK's active site

gly.pfk_restored.text_dramatic: The gatekeeper runs again. The staged fault has been answered — the featured residue set back to glycine, and the healthy wild-type structure brought alongside yours, the two shapes settling into agreement. This is what repair looks like in this story: not a new enzyme, but the old one made whole. The gate swings open, and the split of the sugar lies just ahead.
gly.pfk_restored.text_teaching: This is the PFK restoration reveal — the arc's staged replay of a corrected enzyme, and it is honest about what is real. The mechanics you just watched are real: the game applied a point mutation at residue 209 of the on-screen enzyme (setting it to glycine, GLY), loaded the healthy wild-type cast — PDB 4PFK, 2.40 Å — and superimposed it onto your edited copy (alignment on C-alpha atoms, cmd.super) so the two structures can be compared. The framing is the honest part: the cast is the bacterial enzyme (Geobacillus stearothermophilus), whose own residue 209 is a histidine — the game asserts no bacterial equivalent of the human disease position, so this edit is a symbolic replay, not a structural correction of a real mutation. The human story it stands in for: PFKM G209D abolishes PFK-1 activity in yeast-complementation assays (Raben 1995) and is classified Likely pathogenic in ClinVar (VCV003375341) for Glycogen Storage Disease VII / Tarui disease (MIM:232800) — and in a human enzyme, a fix that restores the glycine at the featured residue is precisely the corrective shape this arc imagines. The road continues: the six-carbon sugar now splits into two three-carbon tracks.

gly.fbp_to_pyruvate.text_dramatic: Aldolase falls like an axe: the six-carbon sugar splits into two three-carbon halves — dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. You ride one twin; the isomerase bends the other onto your track until the two halves run level. Then the assembly line seizes you both — five enzymes in swift succession, each shaving the three carbons toward one coiled destination: phosphoenolpyruvate. The ledger so far: 2 ATP invested + 2 ATP recovered + 2 NADH banked. The second substrate-level ATP is still to come — pyruvate kinase holds it.
gly.fbp_to_pyruvate.text_teaching: Steps 4 through 9, in order. Step 4 — aldolase (class: lyase) cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two three-carbon molecules: dihydroxyacetone phosphate and D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Step 5 — triose phosphate isomerase converts dihydroxyacetone phosphate into D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, so both halves of the split sugar reach the same track. Step 6 — glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase phosphorylates G3P at the 1 carbon to yield the high-energy molecule 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; this is the step that banks NADH. Step 7 — phosphoglycerate kinase makes ATP at the expense of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, yielding ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate (the first substrate-level phosphorylation — one per triose, the 2 invested ATPs recovered). Step 8 — phosphoglycerate mutase converts 3-phosphoglycerate into 2-phosphoglycerate. Step 9 — enolase converts 2-phosphoglycerate into phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP). The account after step 9: 2 ATP invested + 2 ATP recovered + 2 NADH banked — net ATP zero so far. The payoff's second substrate-level ATP does not land here; it lands at pyruvate kinase, the next node.

gly.pyruvate_kinase.text_dramatic: Pyruvate kinase strikes the final blow. Phosphoenolpyruvate — the spring the assembly line wound tight — snaps its phosphate onto ADP, and the second substrate-level ATP is born. What falls away is pyruvate: the three-carbon molecule this whole journey was aimed at. The cell's ledger tips into profit — and for you, the crossroads is one step away.
gly.pyruvate_kinase.text_teaching: Step 10: pyruvate kinase catalyzes the transfer — PEP + ADP -> pyruvate + ATP, the second substrate-level phosphorylation of glycolysis. The step is regulated by the energy in the cell: high concentrations of ATP, acetyl-CoA, alanine, and cAMP all signal 'enough' and inhibit the enzyme. The cast on screen is PDB 7FS3 — human PKLR, the liver-type (L-type) pyruvate kinase, resolved at 1.66 Å in complex with its allosteric modulator, oxalate (a pyruvate analog resting in the active site), Mg2+ and K+ (Nain-Perez 2023). One honest line about tissue types: 7FS3 is the L-type isoform — the liver's version of the enzyme — while the disease below afflicts red blood cells, whose R-type enzyme is built from the same PKLR gene. The disease story: PKLR R479H is classified Pathogenic in ClinVar (VCV000001510) for chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia type 2 / pyruvate kinase deficiency (MIM:266200); the variant is annotated in the Amish population, and UniProt notes it causes no conformational change (VAR_011480; Valentini 2002). Red blood cells depend entirely on glycolysis for their ATP, which is why a sluggish pyruvate kinase shows up as anemia. Researchers have even photographed the mutant itself: PDB 2VGG, the human erythrocyte pyruvate kinase R479H mutant (Valentini 2002) — the same residue the game's pyruvate-kinase edit targets.

choices.label: Examine the pyruvate kinase active site

gly.pyruvate.text_dramatic: Pyruvate. The word the whole road was spelled toward. Ten enzymatic steps behind you; the three-carbon molecule they promised stands before you — and every road forward passes through this point. Ahead, the air itself decides: burn the carbon on through the great furnace while breath holds, or ferment it when the air runs thin. The fork is the very next threshold.
gly.pyruvate.text_teaching: Glycolysis ends at pyruvate — two of them, one from each three-carbon track of the split sugar. What happens next depends on oxygen: aerobically, pyruvate is fed into the citric acid cycle via the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex; anaerobically — when oxygen is absent — it is reduced to lactate or ethanol, using a process known as fermentation. One molecule, and the tissue's breathing decides its fate. The next node is the fork itself.
